questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Asymptotes of a Horizontal Hyperbola Given in Standard Form
questions.problem: Find the asymptotes of the hyperbola $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The standard equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

For a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin, the equations of the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{b}{a}x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
a=\sqrt{4}=2,\,b=\sqrt{16}=4.
$$

Therefore, the asymptotes of the hyperbola are 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \frac{4}{2}x \\  & =\pm 2x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The asymptotes of the hyperbola ${x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}=8$ are$\,\,y=\pm $
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The standard equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

For a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin, the equations of the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{b}{a}x.
$$

To rewrite the given equation in standard form, we divide both sides of the equation by $8$ and then simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2} & =8 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{2{y}^{2}}{8} & =\frac{8}{8} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $a=\sqrt{8}$ and $b=\sqrt{4}=2.$

Therefore, the asymptotes of the hyperbola are 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{8}}x \\  & =\pm \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}}x \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}x \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

To rewrite the given equation in standard form, we divide both sides of the equation by $100$ and then simplify, as follows:

$$

$$

So, we have $a=\sqrt{4}=2,$ and $b=\sqrt{25}=5.$ 

Therefore, the asymptotes are $y=\pm \frac{5}{2}x.$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the asymptotes of the hyperbola $\dfrac{x^2}{36} - \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The standard equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2}=1.
$$

For a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin, the equations of the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \dfrac{b}{a}x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
a=\sqrt{36} = 6, \qquad b=\sqrt9 =3.
$$

Therefore, the asymptotes of the hyperbola are 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \frac{3}{6}x \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}x.\end{aligned}
$$
